name: C
title: C from the first line
intro: C is the language underneath a great deal of everything else: operating systems, the Python and Rust runtimes, and most of the programs on a small computer. It is small, close to the machine, and strict about types. These lessons use C11. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.c and type gcc -std=c11 -o hello hello.c && ./hello.

sections.p: A C program starts in main. printf prints text, but only what you ask for: it does not add a newline unless you write \n. The line #include <stdio.h> brings printf in. return 0 tells the operating system the program finished cleanly.
Everything after // on a line is a comment. A comment between /* and */ can span lines. Comments are for people; the compiler throws them away.

practice.why: printf does not add a space or a newline unless you write them. The second call starts right where the first stopped, then \n ends the line.
The first printf is inside a comment, so it never runs.

practice.q: Where does a C program start?
practice.why: The operating system calls main. printf only prints.

practice.q: What does return 0 from main mean?
options: The program finished without reporting an error
Return to the top of main
practice.answer: The program finished without reporting an error
practice.why: The number returned from main is the program's exit status. Zero is the usual success code.

practice.q: Which line brings printf into the program?
practice.why: stdio.h is the standard header that declares printf.

sections.p: A variable has a type and a name. int holds a whole number. = stores a value; it does not ask whether two things are equal.
When both sides of / are integers, the result is an integer. The fraction is dropped, not rounded. % is the remainder.

practice.why: n starts at 10 and then becomes 10 − 3.
Both 5 and 2 are ints, so / drops the fraction.
% is the remainder. 5 is two 2s, with 1 left over.

practice.q: What does = mean in int n = 4?
practice.why: One equals sign assigns. Two equals signs, ==, compare.

practice.q: Which type holds a whole number?
practice.why: int is the basic integer type. C has no string type of its own; text is an array of char.

sections.p: if runs the next block only when the test is true. == compares two numbers. A single = would store a value instead, which is a different job.

practice.why: n == 2 is true, so only the first branch runs.
In a test, zero is false and any other number is true. n is 0, so the else branch runs.

practice.q: Which operator asks whether two ints are equal?
practice.why: = stores a value. == compares. != asks whether they differ.

practice.q: When does the else block run?
options: When the if test is false
When the if test is true
practice.answer: When the if test is false
practice.why: else is the other branch. It is skipped when the test succeeds.
4 is not greater than 5, but it is greater than 3, so the else if branch runs and the rest is skipped.

sections.p: A for loop has three parts in the brackets: where to start, when to keep going, and what to do after each pass. This prints 0, 1 and 2. When i reaches 3 the test i < 3 fails and the loop stops. continue skips the rest of the current pass and goes straight to the step.
while repeats as long as its test is true. The counter has to change inside the loop, or it never ends.

practice.why: i runs through 1, 2 and 3, and each printf adds a digit with no newline. The newline comes after the loop.
The body runs for n = 0 and n = 1, then n is 2 and the test fails.

practice.q: What are the three parts inside for ( ... )?
practice.why: for (i = 0; i < 3; i = i + 1) sets i, checks it, then moves it after each pass.

practice.q: Why must a while loop change something it tests?
options: Otherwise the test stays true and the loop never ends
The compiler rejects an unchanged variable
The change is what gets printed
practice.answer: Otherwise the test stays true and the loop never ends
practice.why: The test is checked every pass. If nothing it depends on changes, it keeps succeeding.
continue skips the rest of the body for that pass. When i is 2 the printf is skipped, then the loop carries on with 3.

sections.p: A function has a return type, a name, and parameters. add takes two ints and returns an int. The call add(2, 3) runs the body with those values and gives back whatever it returns.

practice.why: twice returns n * 2, and it is called with 4.
A negative argument hits the first return. A positive one falls through to return 1.

practice.q: What does the int before the function name say?
options: The type of the value it returns
practice.answer: The type of the value it returns
practice.why: int add(...) returns an int. The parameter types are written inside the brackets.

options: The function stops and hands a value back to the caller
practice.answer: The function stops and hands a value back to the caller
practice.why: return leaves the function. main's return is special only because main is where the program started.
void means the function returns nothing. Each call prints one line.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Many values of one type, side by side.

sections.p: An array holds a fixed number of values of the same type, one after another in memory. int nuts[5] makes room for five ints. They are numbered from 0, so the last one is nuts[4]. Braces give the starting values.

A for loop from 0 up to (but not including) the length visits every element. C does not store an array's length for you. Inside the function where the array is declared, sizeof nuts / sizeof nuts[0] works it out: the size of the whole array in bytes divided by the size of one element.

sections.h: Passing an array to a function
sections.p: When you pass an array to a function, the function receives only where the array starts, not its length. So C functions that take an array almost always take the length as a second parameter. The function can change the caller's elements, because it works on the same memory.

C does not check that an index is inside the array. Reading nuts[5] from a five-element array is not an error message; it is undefined behaviour: the program may print rubbish, crash, or seem to work and fail later. Many security holes in C programs started this way. Keep the length next to the array and test your loop bounds. Compiling with -fsanitize=address makes gcc and clang stop the program at the first bad access while you test.

practice.why: Indexes start at 0, so a[1] is 20 and a[3] is 40.
Elements without a starting value in the braces are set to 0.

practice.q: Why do C functions that take an array usually take its length too?
options: The function only receives where the array starts
Arrays must always be passed in pairs
sizeof is not allowed inside functions
practice.answer: The function only receives where the array starts
practice.why: Inside the function the array is just a pointer to its first element, so sizeof cannot tell how many there are.

practice.q: What happens if you read past the end of a C array?
options: The program always stops with an error
practice.why: C does not check indexes. Tools such as -fsanitize=address can catch it while testing.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Characters in an array, ending with a zero.

sections.p: C has no separate string type. A string is an array of char that ends with a zero byte, written '\0'. A literal such as "acorn" takes six bytes: five letters and the zero. %s in printf prints characters until it reaches that zero, and strlen from <string.h> counts them.
sections.out:
acorn has 5 letters
the array takes 6 bytes
first letter a

sections.p: Because a string is an array, you can loop over it and change single characters. The loop stops at the zero. toupper from <ctype.h> turns one letter into a capital.

== on two strings compares where they are stored, not their letters, so use strcmp: it returns 0 when they are equal. To build a string, snprintf works like printf but writes into an array, and it never writes more than the size you give it, so it cannot run past the end. It returns how many characters the whole text needed, so a result at least as big as the size tells you it was cut short. Older functions such as strcpy and strcat do not check the size, which is why careful code avoids them.
sections.out:
same letters
oak tree #7
Douglas fir tre (needed 23)

practice.why: strlen counts the 4 letters. The array also holds the zero at the end, so it is 5 bytes.
%s stops at the first zero byte, which is now at index 3.

practice.q: How should you check whether two C strings have the same letters?
practice.why: == compares the addresses where the strings are stored, not their contents.

practice.q: Why is snprintf safer than strcpy for building a string?
options: It never writes more than the size you pass
practice.answer: It never writes more than the size you pass
practice.why: strcpy keeps copying until the source ends, even past the end of the destination.

lessons.title: Pointers
lessons.summary: Variables that hold where something is.

sections.p: Every variable lives at an address in memory. &x gives the address of x, and a pointer is a variable that stores such an address. int *p declares a pointer to an int. Writing *p follows the pointer to the value it points at, so *p = 7 changes x itself.
sections.out:
x is 3, *p is 3
x is now 7

sections.h: Letting a function change your variables
sections.p: C passes arguments by value: a function gets copies. To let it change the caller's variables, pass their addresses. This is how scanf stores what it reads, and how a function can hand back more than one result.

An array's name used in an expression becomes a pointer to its first element. Adding 1 to a pointer moves it to the next element, not the next byte, so *(p + 2) and p[2] mean the same thing. That is why passing an array to a function passes only its start.

A pointer that points at nothing is set to NULL. Following a NULL pointer, or one that points at memory that no longer exists, is undefined behaviour and usually crashes the program. Functions that may fail to find something often return NULL, so check before you use the result.

practice.why: p points at a, so *p = *p + 10 changes a itself.
bump changes only its own copy. bump_ptr follows the address to x, so only that call counts.
v + 1 points at the second element (4), and p[1] is the one after it (6).
& takes an address; * follows one.

lessons.title: Structs
lessons.summary: Grouping related values under one name.

sections.p: A struct bundles several values, each with its own name and type, into one. Fields are reached with a dot. typedef gives the struct a short name so you can write Tree instead of struct tree. Structs can be copied with = and passed to and returned from functions like any other value.
sections.out:
oak: 120 nuts, 18.5 m
copy has 0, original still has 120

sections.p: An array of structs is the C way to keep a table of records. Designated initializers such as .nuts = 40 name each field, which reads well and keeps working if the fields are reordered.

Passing a big struct by value copies all of it, and the function cannot change the caller's copy. Passing a pointer avoids both problems. p->nuts is shorthand for (*p).nuts: follow the pointer, then take the field. Mark the pointer const when the function only reads.
sections.out:
oak has 18 nuts
oak has 0 nuts

practice.why: b = a copies the whole struct, so changing b leaves a alone.
add receives a pointer, so both calls change the same Box: 1 + 5 + 5.

options: (*p).field: follow the pointer, then take the field
Copy the struct p into field
practice.answer: (*p).field: follow the pointer, then take the field
practice.why: -> is shorthand for following a pointer to a struct and reading one field.

lessons.title: Memory with malloc and free
lessons.summary: Asking for memory while the program runs.

sections.p: Local variables disappear when their function returns, and arrays need a size fixed when you write the program. When you only know the size while running, ask for memory with malloc from <stdlib.h>. It returns a pointer to a block of the size you ask for, or NULL if there is none. The memory stays yours until you hand it back with free.

realloc resizes a block, moving it if it has to, and returns the new address. A common pattern is a list that doubles its capacity whenever it fills up, so adding n items costs only about 2n copies in total. Keep the old pointer until realloc succeeds, so a failure does not lose your data.
sections.out:
grew to 2
grew to 4
grew to 8
grew to 16
9 items, last 81

sections.p: The C compiler does not track who owns which block, so a few mistakes are easy to make. Forgetting free is a leak: the memory stays taken until the program ends. Using a pointer after free (a dangling pointer) or freeing the same block twice is undefined behaviour. A good habit is that whoever calls malloc is responsible for the matching free, and to set the pointer to NULL afterwards. Tools such as Valgrind and -fsanitize=address find these mistakes while you test. Languages such as Rust were designed largely to make them impossible.

practice.why: calloc, unlike malloc, fills the new block with zeros.

practice.q: What does malloc return when there is no memory left?
practice.why: Always check the result before using it.

options: Memory taken with malloc that is never freed
Reading past the end of an array
practice.answer: Memory taken with malloc that is never freed
practice.why: The block stays reserved until the program ends, so a long-running program slowly uses more and more.

practice.q: Why keep the old pointer when calling realloc?
options: If realloc fails it returns NULL and the old block is still yours
realloc always frees the old block
The new pointer is always the same
practice.answer: If realloc fails it returns NULL and the old block is still yours
practice.why: Writing p = realloc(p, ...) would lose the only pointer to your data when it fails.

lessons.title: Project: a nut ledger
lessons.summary: Structs, arrays, strings and sorting in one small program.

sections.p: This small program puts the earlier lessons together. It reads a day-by-day record of where nuts were buried, adds up each tree with a loop over an array of structs, sorts the totals with the standard library's qsort, and prints a report. qsort sorts any array: you give it the start, the number of elements, the size of one, and a comparison function that says which of two elements comes first. The function gets const void * pointers, which can point at anything, so it converts them back to const Total * first.

Change the program and check the output still makes sense: add a column with each tree's share of the total as a percentage, read the entries from a file with fopen and fscanf instead of an array, or replace the fixed totals[8] with the growing list from the memory lesson so any number of trees fits.

practice.q: What should a qsort comparison function return when a should come before b?
practice.why: Negative means a first, positive means b first, and zero means they are equal for sorting.
up returns a negative number when a is smaller, so smaller values come first.

practice.q: Why does by_nuts take const void * parameters?
options: qsort works with any element type, so it passes untyped pointers
void means the function returns nothing
Because Total cannot be passed to functions
practice.answer: qsort works with any element type, so it passes untyped pointers
practice.why: The comparison converts them back to the real type before reading the fields.
